fieldProfiles.title: Moral reasons and authority
fieldProfiles.text: Evolutionary explanations of cooperative dispositions do not by themselves explain the authority of moral reasons. Natural selection may account for sympathy, but its causal history does not establish why powerful agents remain answerable to the weak. Theism can ground equal moral standing by treating persons as ends intended by a rational creator. Yet this proposal succeeds only if divine intention explains normativity better than secular moral realism; it cannot simply assume that commands generate obligations. This comparison preserves the crucial distinction between explaining moral psychology and justifying moral authority.

fieldProfiles.title: Experience under comparison
fieldProfiles.text: Religious experience can be discussed rationally once its evidential limits are made explicit. Recurring features, considered psychological alternatives, and morally transformative effects may raise the experiencer’s personal probability of theism without establishing certainty. Convergence across independent experiences could add cumulative weight, though selection effects and conflicts among traditions must remain part of the comparison. This approach respects the distinction between sincerity and public proof while recognizing that private evidence need not be epistemically worthless to the person who undergoes it.

fieldProfiles.title: Order without gap filling
fieldProfiles.text: The appeal to order need not depend on gaps in current scientific explanation. Mathematically describable laws, stable causal regularities, and minds capable of discovering them together invite a deeper question about why reality is intelligible. A personal source gains support only comparatively, if it makes this intelligibility more expected than brute law does without adding unsupported claims about intervention or scripture. Scientific progress therefore does not necessarily dissolve the argument; it reveals more of the stable structure whose ultimate modal explanation remains genuinely contested.

fieldProfiles.title: Religious diversity as evidence
fieldProfiles.text: Conflicting religious experiences weaken any simple inference from felt presence to a particular supernatural source. If equally sincere people report incompatible revelations, sincerity cannot identify which interpretation is true without an independent method. The diversity is more expected if culture and psychology shape experience than if one personal deity reliably communicates a stable message. This does not prove that every experience is naturalistic, but it gives Hitchens a comparative likelihood argument rather than the categorical assertion that supernatural evidence is simply nonexistent.

fieldProfiles.title: Correctability beats authority
fieldProfiles.text: A secular moral framework can claim an institutional advantage without implying that unbelievers are better people. Public reasons remain open to revision through evidence, testimony from harmed parties, and reciprocal criticism, whereas alleged divine commands can make error sacred and resistant to correction. The relevant comparison is not crime rates among believers and atheists, but how each system detects and repairs moral mistakes. Correctability is itself a moral virtue because it reduces the duration and reach of confidently imposed harm.

fieldProfiles.title: Suffering and expected worlds
fieldProfiles.text: The problem of suffering becomes sharper when framed comparatively. A world shaped by indifferent evolutionary and geological processes predicts waste, extinction, disease, and uneven catastrophe without further assumptions. A world governed by a perfectly powerful and loving personal being requires additional explanations for why those same patterns are necessary or permitted. Natural causes do not by themselves disprove God, but their expected fit under naturalism and surprising severity under benevolent supervision can shift the evidential balance against the greatness claim.
